narrativeProgression.description: Introductory scene sets the stage for a political interview. Guest shares her motivation for running for Secretary of State, highlighting voter disillusionment with 'politics as usual' and a desire for increased engagement and transparency. She emphasizes the importance of her previous experience in campaigning and understanding voter sentiment.
Stephanie Thomas states her main motivation for running for office is restoring faith in government through increased engagement and transparency.
She asserts that the next Secretary of State has a crucial opportunity to foster trust in government.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Stephanie Thomas addresses critical aspects of voter disengagement and education, emphasizing the role of government in fostering civic responsibility.

keyMoments.changeDescription: The mood shifts from calm to serious as the visual of civic education signs underlines the gravity of voter education.

narrativeProgression.description: Stephanie Thomas delves into the issue of voter education, arguing that the lack thereof is a major contributing factor to voter apathy and distrust in government. She connects low voter turnout, especially in local elections, to the lack of understanding about how government works and how individual votes matter. She asserts that the responsibility of educating citizens about civic duty lies not only in the education system but also in the government itself.
Stephanie Thomas contends that the country is at a critical juncture due to the increasing voter apathy.
She uses low voter turnout in municipal elections as evidence of this problem, highlighting the fact that 30% participation is considered 'high'.
She emphasizes that both voter registration and voter access are important but mean little if voters lack the motivation and understanding to exercise their right.

Stephanie Thomas emphasizes the importance of her 'eclectic background', hinting at her unique qualifications for the role.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hello, I'm Bruce Conroy and I am Tarek and tonight on Community Conversation to Stephanie
Thomas, who is running for Secretary of State.
For over the start off of what made you want to run for Secretary of State?
The reason I'm running for Secretary of State, I have many, but one of them is I really
believe what I learned when I was campaigning in 2018 is that many people are tired of
politics as usual.
They find it difficult to assess our democracy.
They don't know how or they lose faith in the people they voted for.
And I think the next Secretary of State has a real opportunity to engage with people,
to really go into the community, speak with everyone from town clerks to registrars
of voters.
But also chambers of commerce, small business development centers, advocacy groups.
I really feel that the electorate, if you will, has lost touch with how to engage with
government.
And I think that is part of the reason we're seeing such distrust in apathy.
One thing I talk about a lot is just educating people.
I do believe we're at an inflection point.
We have always had apathy at the polls, municipal elections.
If someone typically gets 30% turnout, that's considered high.
That's very troubling.
Prior to Trump's election, I think even nationally 60 something percent turnout, I think that's
abysmal.
And then you take one more factor, which is the lack of civic education.
And I can't tell you how many people in a certain generation never had any civic settle.
And most people who had it will say they had too little of it.
So I think all of those things are creating a reality in our democracy that 10 years from
now, I don't think we want to see where that goes.
And I think we have spent as a country, indefinitely as a state, putting all of our effort into voter
registration and voter expanded voter access, which both are very important.
But if you ignore those other pieces, I think we're doing ourselves a disservice because
you can have as many people able to vote.
But if they don't want to, you can't force them.
So I really think the next secretary has an opportunity to hopefully stand up something
that could be replicated in other states, because this isn't a Connecticut problem.
But something that focuses on civic education and civic engagement, not only just for kids,
but for adults as well, because guess what?
They vote.
And their voice should be heard.
I have often said, we don't even know what we want as a nation because enough people
don't vote to tell us.
And I find that just very troubling and a sign that our democracy is on the wrong path.
So I do think that's a differentiator, but to answer your question more specifically,
I have a eclectic background, if you will, as a small business owner, as someone who has
worked in or for the nonprofit sector for the last 30 years.
And now as a legislator, it has created a very robust background that doptails very
nicely with the role of the office.
And I get excited talking about transparency and efficiency in government.
And my masters is in nonprofit management and sort of a sub specialty and organizational
development.
These are things that I find exciting.
My legislative role also has taught me how to navigate Hartford, which I do think is important.
And I'll say it here because on the campaign trail, I think people get shiny object syndrome
and everything is about sound bites and making it sound sexy.
But this job is actually not sexy at all.
It's a lot about data and lawyers, answering questions and behind the scenes, management
of information.
And I think, you know, we always focus on what comes next, but I think actually right
now where we are in history, culture, the pandemic, the next secretary has a lot to take
on over the next four years, implementing things that we've already passed.
Automatic voter registration comes to mind, but we need to sit down with all of these state
agencies that we have now enabled to do automatic voter registration, but they're not ready

And there's work to be done there.
We've just gotten a report back about risk limiting audits and some work we need to do

That needs to be looked at, implemented early voting misinformation.

it's so prevalent in cybersecurity.
These are all big issues in and of themselves.
So I would just like to say we have to remember both sides of the job.
Yes, the visionary side, but there's also the implementation side and better to do a
few things really well than a lot of things.
